title: Life moves onto land
summary: Between about 470 and 300 million years ago the bare continents were taken over, first by tiny plants and millipedes, then by forests, four-legged animals, flying insects and the first egg-layers on dry land. This story follows that conquest from the earliest spores to the collapse of the great coal rainforests.

chapters.title: First spores on a bare land
chapters.text: For most of Earth's history the land was bare rock, sand and mud, with no more life on it than thin films and crusts of microbes; fossils from lake beds a billion years old show such life on land. Plants grew out of green algae that lived in fresh water. The first sign of them is their spores: tiny grains with tough walls, about 470 million years old, found in rocks in Argentina and, about ten million years later, in Saudi Arabia and Czechia. The plants that shed them were probably small and low, and their bodies do not turn up as fossils for another 40 million years.
species: Cryptospores (spores of the first land plants)

sites.name: Early Middle Ordovician spore beds, Argentina
sites.note: A mix of five kinds of plant spores, the oldest accepted trace of land plants.

images.caption: A dark, knobbly biological soil crust on bare desert ground in Utah, a living hint of how the land may have looked before plants.
images.note: A present-day desert crust in Utah, USA; today's crusts include organisms that did not yet exist, so Ordovician crusts were probably simpler.

images.caption: Clumps of dark living soil crust spread over red sand in Canyonlands National Park, Utah.
images.note: Present-day crust with modern grasses and flowers, which did not exist 470 million years ago.

chapters.evidenceNote: Spores with tough walls survive where soft plants rot away; the 470-million-year-old spores from Argentina are widely accepted as coming from land plants, but older spore-like fossils, some from the Cambrian, may come from algae on their way to becoming plants.

sources.title: Europe PMC record: Early Middle Ordovician evidence for land plants in Argentina (Rubinstein et al., New Phytologist 2010)

chapters.title: Cooksonia, the first plants with pipes
chapters.text: Cooksonia was a plant only a few centimetres tall: a bare stalk that forked a few times, with no leaves and no roots, each branch tipped with a little capsule of spores. In at least one kind a dark strand runs up the middle of the stem, the earliest known tissue for carrying water. Water pipes like these would later let plants grow tall. Some of the oldest Cooksonia come from Ireland and Wales, where tiny zircon crystals dated in 2024 show the rocks are no older than about 426 to 427 million years; a Cooksonia from Czechia may be about 432 million years old.

sites.note: Cooksonia in Silurian rocks no older than about 426 million years.

chapters.title: Millipedes and scorpions creep ashore
chapters.place: Isle of Kerrera, near Oban, Scotland
chapters.text: Animals followed the plants onto land. Kampecaris, a small millipede from old lake beds on the Scottish island of Kerrera, about 425 million years old, is one of the oldest land animals known and may have fed on rotting plants, as most millipedes do today. A younger millipede from Stonehaven, Pneumodesmus, about 414 million years old, has breathing holes along its body, so it must have breathed air. Scorpions were around even earlier: Dolichophonus, from the Pentland Hills near Edinburgh and 436 to 428 million years old, is the oldest scorpion known, though nobody can yet say whether it lived on land or in water.

chapters.title: A whole world frozen in stone
chapters.text: Near Rhynie in Scotland, hot springs rich in silica flooded a marshy plain and turned its life to stone where it stood, down to single cells. The plants, such as Rhynia and Aglaophyton, were leafless green stems, and inside them are the oldest known mycorrhizal fungi, the partner fungi that live in plant roots to this day. Mites, springtails, harvestmen and spider-like trigonotarbids lived among the stems. Rising a metre or more above everything else was Prototaxites, a trunk-like column long thought to be a giant fungus; a 2026 study argued that it was neither fungus nor plant but a lost branch of life.

sites.name: Rhynie chert, Aberdeenshire
sites.note: A hot-spring ecosystem preserved cell by cell.

images.caption: A polished piece of Rhynie chert crowded with round cross-sections of Rhynia stems, turned to stone where they grew about 410 million years ago.
images.note: The scale bar is 1 cm.

images.caption: Drawings of six Rhynie chert plants, including Rhynia (A), Aglaophyton (B) and the leafy Asteroxylon (D), small leafless or scaly stems with spore capsules.

chapters.evidenceNote: Silica from the springs filled the cells before they could rot, so thin slices of the chert show plants, fungi and animals under the microscope; only Prototaxites' place in the tree of life is still argued over.

chapters.title: The first forests rise
chapters.place: Sea cliffs near Minehead, Somerset, England
chapters.text: In 2024 scientists described fossil tree trunks, fallen branches and roots in sandstone cliffs on the Somerset coast, about 390 million years old: the oldest forest yet found. Its trees, Calamophyton, looked a little like tree ferns, with a crown of twigs on a slender trunk up to about 4 metres tall, and the branches they shed littered the forest floor. A few million years later forests at Cairo and Gilboa in New York State held Wattieza trees 8 metres or more tall and Archaeopteris, whose extensive, spreading roots were much like those of modern trees. Roots broke up rock and carried carbon deeper into the soil, and as forests spread, carbon dioxide in the air fell steeply.

chapters.title: A fish with a neck and wrists
chapters.text: Shallow streams in what is now Arctic Canada, then close to the equator, were home to Tiktaalik, a fish up to about 2.7 metres long. It had scales, fins and gills, but also a neck, strong bones like a wrist inside its front fins and probably simple lungs, so it could prop itself up in shallow water. Found in 2004, it shows the body of four-legged animals taking shape inside a fish. It was a cousin of the first four-legged animals rather than their ancestor: footprints in a Polish quarry, about 390 million years old, suggest that animals with legs were already walking more than ten million years earlier, though some experts think fish made the marks.

sites.name: Fram Formation, Ellesmere Island
sites.note: Where Tiktaalik was found in 2004.

sites.name: Zachełmie quarry, Holy Cross Mountains, Poland
sites.note: Footprints claimed as the oldest tracks of four-legged animals.

chapters.evidenceNote: Tiktaalik's bones are not in doubt; what is argued over is whether the older Polish footprints were made by four-legged animals, as their finders Grzegorz Niedźwiedzki and Per Ahlberg hold, or by fish, as Spencer Lucas has argued.

chapters.title: Crisis in the Devonian seas
chapters.text: About 372 million years ago, and again about 359, the seas ran short of oxygen and black, lifeless mud settled on the sea floor. The first crisis, named after the Kellwasser valley in Germany, wiped out the great reefs built by corals and sponge-like stromatoporoids and perhaps 40 percent of sea species; the second ended the armoured placoderm fishes. One idea blames the new forests: deep roots broke up rock, rivers carried the freed nutrients to the sea, and blooms of algae used up the oxygen. Tiktaalik's kind, the fish with necks and wrists, died out, while the true four-legged animals came through.

sites.name: Kellwassertal, Harz mountains
sites.note: Dark limestone layers that name the first crisis.

images.caption: The Kellwasser stream in the Harz mountains of Germany, whose valley gave its name to the first great Late Devonian extinction.
A block of Kellwasser limestone about 372 million years old, packed with shells, on show at the Geoeducation Centre in Kielce, Poland.
images.note: Shown in Kielce, Poland; the file page does not say where the block was collected.

chapters.evidenceNote: Black shales and the sudden loss of reef fossils show the crises happened; their cause is argued over, with nutrients from the first forests (Thomas Algeo and Stephen Scheckler), volcanic eruptions and a cooling climate all proposed.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: The Devonian Period

chapters.title: Many-toed legs in Greenland
chapters.text: After the crisis four-legged animals spread. In the mountains of East Greenland, in rocks about 365 million years old, lie Acanthostega, about 60 cm long with eight webbed fingers on each hand and gills like a fish, and Ichthyostega, about 1.5 metres long with seven toes on each hind foot. Acanthostega probably spent nearly all its life in shallow, weedy water, which suggests that legs with toes first evolved for water, not for walking. Ichthyostega could drag itself over flat ground on its strong front legs, moving more like a seal than a salamander.

chapters.title: Seeds free plants from water
chapters.text: Spore plants have a weak spot: their sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg, which ties them to damp ground. Seed plants got round it. The oldest known seeds, about 365 million years old from West Virginia, belong to Elkinsia, whose young seeds sat in small cup-shaped cases. A seed wraps a baby plant and its food in a coat that keeps it from drying out, so it can wait for rain before it sprouts, and pollen carries the sperm through the air. Seed plants could now grow on dry slopes where spore plants failed, and their descendants dominate the land today.

sites.name: Hampshire Formation near Elkins, Randolph County
sites.note: Young seeds of Elkinsia, the oldest known seed plant.

images.caption: A fossil of Elkinsia polymorpha from West Virginia, about 365 million years old, the oldest known seed plant.
images.note: On show in the Museo de Paleobotánica Roberto Wagner, Córdoba, Spain. The small seeds and their cup-like cases are hard to see at this size.

images.caption: A drawing of Runcaria from Belgium, about 385 million years old: a spore case wrapped in a cup of lobes, an early step towards the seed.
images.note: The structure is only a few millimetres long (scale bar 1 mm).

chapters.evidenceNote: Seeds with their cup-like cases are preserved in Late Devonian rocks; Runcaria from Belgium, about 385 million years old, shows an earlier, not yet fully wrapped stage.

chapters.title: Insects become the first flyers
chapters.place: Bitterfeld and Delitzsch, Saxony-Anhalt and Saxony, Germany
chapters.text: Insects were the first animals to fly. The oldest fossils of winged insects are about 328 to 324 million years old, and they already come in several kinds, so flight probably began earlier. One of the oldest, Delitzschala from eastern Germany, had wings spanning just 2.5 cm, still showing their spots. By the end of the Carboniferous, griffinflies such as Meganeura from France had wings spanning about 70 cm, among the largest flying insects ever. A popular idea is that oxygen-rich air let them grow so big, but some recent studies doubt the link.

sites.name: Bitterfeld and Delitzsch area
sites.note: Delitzschala, one of the oldest known winged insects.

sites.name: Commentry coal mines, Allier, France

images.caption: Drawings of Late Carboniferous and Early Permian winged insects and their young, from France and Mazon Creek, many with boldly patterned wings.

chapters.evidenceNote: Wings are the toughest part of an insect and are pressed into the rock with their veins; gene-based estimates put the start of flight much earlier, near 400 million years ago, but no such fossils are known.

chapters.title: Eggs for dry land at Joggins
chapters.place: Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Nova Scotia, Canada
chapters.text: At Joggins in Nova Scotia, sea cliffs cut through a coal forest of giant clubmoss trees up to 30 metres tall. Inside their hollow fossil stumps lie small animals that seem to have fallen in and been trapped, among them Hylonomus, a lizard-like animal about 20 to 25 cm long that probably ate millipedes and early insects. It was long called the oldest reptile. Reptiles, mammals and their kin, the amniotes, lay eggs with a shell and inner bags of fluid that keep the young from drying out, so they could breed far from water. A 2025 study placed Hylonomus just outside the amniotes, so who laid the first such eggs is an open question again.

sites.name: Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Chignecto Bay
sites.note: Fossil tree stumps holding early four-legged animals.

images.caption: The Joggins Fossil Cliffs on the shore of Chignecto Bay, Nova Scotia, where layers of a Carboniferous coal forest are exposed.
A fossil clubmoss tree trunk, probably Sigillaria, still standing upright in the Joggins cliffs where it grew, with a rock hammer for scale.
images.note: Hollow stumps like this one trapped Hylonomus and other small animals.

images.caption: Hylonomus, a lizard-like animal about 20 to 25 cm long from Joggins, long counted as the oldest known reptile.
images.note: Colours are guessed.

chapters.evidenceNote: Hylonomus's bones are well known, but whether it was a true amniote is argued over, and 350-million-year-old clawed footprints from Australia, claimed in 2025 as amniote tracks, may have been made by other animals.

chapters.title: A coal-swamp shore in ironstone
chapters.place: Mazon Creek, near Morris, Illinois, USA
chapters.text: By now swamp forests of giant clubmosses, ferns, horsetails and seed ferns covered the warm lowlands, and their buried remains became the coal that gave the Carboniferous its name. At Mazon Creek in Illinois, plants and animals that washed into a muddy bay about 309 million years ago were quickly sealed inside ironstone nodules. Split open, the nodules show more than 400 kinds of plants and over 320 kinds of animals: insects, the giant millipede relative Arthropleura, early four-legged animals and the strange Tully monster. Few places show so fully what lived in and around a coal forest.

sites.name: Mazon Creek and the Braidwood strip mines
sites.note: Ironstone nodules from the Francis Creek Shale.

images.caption: An ironstone nodule from Mazon Creek split in two to show both halves of a Tully monster, Tullimonstrum, in the Natural History Museum of Milan.
An artist's reconstruction of the Tully monster, with eyes on a crossbar and a long snout ending in toothed jaws.
images.note: What kind of animal Tullimonstrum was is still argued over, so its appearance is uncertain.

images.caption: Fronds of the seed fern Neuropteris from a coal-mine spoil heap near Essex, Illinois, part of the Mazon Creek fossil beds.
images.note: On show at the Field Museum, Chicago.

chapters.evidenceNote: Bacteria rotting the buried bodies made the iron mineral siderite, which cast them in hard nodules, often with their soft parts.

chapters.title: The coal rainforests break apart
chapters.place: Former Riola and Vermilion Grove coal mines, near Danville, Illinois, USA
chapters.text: In coal mines near Danville, Illinois, miners and geologists found a whole fossil forest of giant clubmosses, tree ferns, seed ferns and horsetails spread over about 1,000 hectares, drowned when the ground dropped below sea level. Not long afterwards, around 305 million years ago, a short, sharp ice age dried and cooled the tropics, and the great rainforests broke up into patches. The giant clubmoss trees almost vanished and tree ferns took over. Many amphibians died out, while amniotes, with their shelled eggs, coped better with the drier world, and among them were the first synapsids, the line that would one day lead to mammals.

sites.name: Riola and Vermilion Grove mines, near Danville
sites.note: A coal forest drowned just before the collapse, preserved over about 1,000 hectares.

sites.name: Florence, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia
sites.note: Archaeothyris, one of the oldest known synapsids.

images.caption: A drawing of Lepidodendron, a giant clubmoss tree of the coal forests, with a tall scaly trunk, a branching crown and spreading roots.
images.note: Trees like this almost vanished from the tropical swamps around 305 million years ago.

chapters.evidenceNote: Fossil plants and coal layers show the clubmoss forests collapsing; Sarda Sahney, Michael Benton and Howard Falcon-Lang (2010) argued this split animals into isolated pockets and drove their evolution, but Emma Dunne and colleagues (2018) found no sign of such isolation once uneven fossil collecting is allowed for.
